summary:
FLARE (Scientific Intelligence Platform for Spacecraft Fire Safety) is an AI-assisted research platform developed to help researchers understand fire behaviour in microgravity environments. It addresses NASA’s *Flame in Freefall* challenge by bringing together experimental data and scientific documents from NASA research, including the BASS-II experiments.

The platform provides an interactive dashboard for exploring experimental conditions, analysing atmospheric measurements, examining flame behaviour, comparing experimental conditions, and retrieving supporting scientific evidence. Its AI research assistant uses a local language model alongside deterministic scientific analysis and claim validation to generate evidence-grounded explanations while identifying uncertainty and limitations.

Understanding combustion in microgravity is essential because flames, heat, oxygen transport, and smoke behave differently in space than on Earth. These differences can affect fire detection, material selection, and crew safety aboard spacecraft. FLARE aims to make existing research easier to explore, interpret, and trace back to its original evidence, supporting more informed spacecraft fire-safety research.
details:
FLARE (Scientific Intelligence Platform for Spacecraft Fire Safety) is an AI-assisted scientific research platform designed to help researchers investigate and understand combustion behaviour in microgravity environments. It addresses NASA's Flame in Freefall challenge by making spacecraft fire research data easier to explore, analyse, compare, and interpret.

How it works:
FLARE integrates NASA experimental datasets, including BASS-II research data, with relevant scientific documents. Its interactive dashboard provides dedicated modules for exploring experiments, analysing atmospheric measurements, investigating flame behaviour, comparing experimental conditions, and retrieving scientific evidence. Users can also interact with an AI Research Assistant to ask scientific questions. The system combines deterministic Python-based analysis, document retrieval, and a locally running language model. A scientific claim-validation layer checks generated findings against validated analytical results and supporting evidence. It also communicates uncertainty and identifies unsupported conclusions rather than presenting speculation as fact.

Benefits and intended impact:
In microgravity, combustion behaves differently because buoyancy-driven convection is significantly reduced, affecting flame shape, oxygen transport, heat transfer, and fire behaviour. Understanding these differences is important for spacecraft material selection, fire-safety research, and protecting astronauts during long-duration space missions. FLARE helps reduce the effort required to navigate complex research resources and makes scientific findings more accessible, traceable, and understandable.

Technology used:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and interactive data visualisation.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Scientific computing: Pandas, NumPy, and SciPy.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy, and Alembic.
  • AI: Ollama with the Qwen 2.5 3B local language model.
  • Document processing: PDF extraction, text chunking, and PostgreSQL full-text search.
  • Development environment: Windows, Visual Studio Code, and local GPU-based model execution.

Creativity and design considerations:
The key innovation is combining scientific data analysis, evidence retrieval, and AI-assisted explanations in one platform. Instead of relying on an unrestricted chatbot, FLARE separates measured experimental results from derived findings, scientific references, and hypotheses. We considered scientific accuracy, data provenance, reproducibility, uncertainty, experimental limitations, and responsible AI usage throughout development. The platform is designed as a research-support tool, not a certified spacecraft fire-prediction or safety-control system.
